item.title: Families Turn to Symbolic Cremation After Nepal Floods
item.description:
The funeral pyres at Kathmandu’s riverfront temple have been burning steadily. But instead of bodies, it is effigies they have set ablaze — shaped out of sacred grass, as if to conjure something tangible of the loved ones who disappeared in Nepal’s devastating floods.

Nine days after the walls of mud and debris tore through a Himalayan valley along the border of Nepal and Tibet, wiping out entire towns, the death toll stands at more than 1,200. Relatives of 5,000 others who are missing have searched hospital to hospital, waiting and waiting, hoping for a miracle — or closure at least.

On Friday, rescuers were racing to recover survivors among dozens of people believed to have been found trapped in a tunnel. But to many whose loved ones are among the missing, resignation has begun to set in. According to Hindu rituals in Nepal, the mourning period after a death is 13 days. If the rites are not performed before the 10th day, the clock resets.

Some families, accepting that they may never receive the actual remains, have chosen to perform a symbolic cremation of a figure made of bundles of kusha grass. Nearly 300 effigy cremations have taken place at the temple during the past three days, temple officials said.

Among the solemn onlookers on Thursday at the temple in Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal, was Darshan Bhattarai, 15, who came to carry out the last rites for his father, Pushpa Raj Bhattarai, 46, one of the thousands dead or missing.

Darshan had been living in the city with his mother, Kamala, and attending a private school thanks to the salary earned by his father, about $300 a month, relatives said. In search of a better life, the family had first moved from Nepal’s eastern hills to the southern plains, where Mr. Bhattarai for years ran a retail shop. About a decade ago, he got a job as an administrative assistant in Nepal’s hydropower sector. He was posted in one of the projects in Trishuli, an area devastated by the floods last week.

Nepal’s hydroelectric projects experienced some of the worst damage from the floods, caused by a glacial collapse that cascaded into an overwhelming rush of mud, gravel and water. Some workers were swept away. Others were trapped in tunnels. Teams of rescue workers have spent days trying to find a way in.

“When his phone went off, we knew something was wrong,” Sukhdev Khanal, a relative of Mr. Bhattarai’s, said. “One of his colleagues had gone out for a smoke, and he survived. He told us later that the rest were swept away.”

After a week of no news, hope dimmed. So Mr. Bhattarai’s family came to the temple in Kathmandu, Pashupatinath Temple, before the 10th day passed, to perform the cremation on the banks of the Bagmati River.

Darshan arrived with his mother and other family and friends. The priest, Rishi Neupane, came with the necessary items for the cremation: kusha grass, kindling wood, rice, ghee and marigolds. A piece of cloth to serve as a shroud. Darshan and his family watched as Mr. Neupune twisted and bound bundles of the grass until it resembled a large straw doll.

As is customary, Darshan’s head had to be shaved as an act of purification before he could perform the ceremony.

He went to a tap on the side of the temple, ran his head under the water and sat on the edge of stair, as a neighbor used a razor and began shaving lock after lock. Darshan giggled as one of his young cousins felt his shaved head, caressing the tuft of hair that is usually left at the crown, a tender moment before the ceremony.

Then, the priest began his work, laying a printed photo of Mr. Bhattarai on a bamboo stretcher and placing the effigy on top.

Through two hours of rituals, Darshan’s face was blank, even when the rain started lashing. Darshan and some of the relatives pulled back, seeking refuge under a ledge, as the priest, and half a dozen men continued. Mr. Bhattarai’s sister-in-law, umbrella in hand, made a video call to his elderly parents in the village, showing them the effigy.

As the rain poured down, Darshan and the men lowered the effigy into the river, for a cleansing bath, as people took turns paying respects to the photo of Mr. Bhattarai.

Praveen Bhattarai, 40, a childhood friend of Mr. Bhattarai’s, was among the mourners. He said he had last seen him during a visit home for the Dussehra festival last year. They had played cards. Mr. Bhattarai was someone who always kept the mood light, he said.

“Doing the last rites like this is very difficult for the family,” Praveen Bhattarai said. “Somewhere, in the depth of their heart, the question will always be there — that maybe he is alive.”

The family lifted the stretcher and walked in a procession, through the thick smoke of other burning pyres, crossing a bridge over the river to the stone platform where Mr. Bhattarai’s pyre would be set.

Darshan lit the fire.

As his uncle steadied him from behind, the young man walked around the effigy as it burned, followed by his mother. They watched it turn to ash, and then Darshan stepped down to submerge some of the ashes in the river.

As the priest read a final prayer from his mobile phone, the family and friends used water from the river to purify the platform where the cremation had taken place.

Mother and son, with relatives holding their arms, slowly made their way through the temple grounds. As they exited, they passed a large group of pilgrims — dancing to drums, singing “Om namah Shiva!” in praise of the god whose spiritual home is nearby.

They kept going, with Darshan almost being pulled by his uncle, as if sleepwalking into a heavy future.

item.title: Grand Theft Porter: Thieves Steal 800 Barrels of Guinness in Britain
item.description:
The police in the county of Cheshire in northwestern England are investigating the theft of two trailers of Guinness beer from an industrial park.

Two trucks entered the depot on Monday and hauled away trailers containing 800 barrels of the creamy dark stout, the authorities said.

“It is famously said that ‘Guinness is good for you,’ but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for,” Detective Sgt. Gary McClatchey of the Cheshire Constabulary said in a statement on Thursday.

The police will settle for “nothing less than the full recovery of all the items stolen,” he added.

Diageo, the British beverage company that owns Guinness, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokesman for the Cheshire police said on Friday that there were no updates in the investigation.

Precisely what the thieves planned to do with their large stash of stout was unclear. The police said the value of the stolen beer was 115,000 pounds, or about $155,000.

The truck drivers were believed to men, the police said. They appealed for any witnesses to come forward and for motorists to review dashboard camera footage in hopes of catching the brew burglars.

The theft came on the heels of another high-profile beer heist in the United States. Last month, Pabst Blue Ribbon said that 40,000 pounds of its beer had been stolen from a distribution center in Montclair, Calif., a haul that the local police said was worth $25,000.

Pabst offered a reward on social media to anyone who helped them recover the lost beer.

item.title: Iran’s State Media Says U.S. Missiles Hit Iranian Oil Tanker Near Kharg
item.description:
Iran’s state media said Saturday that U.S. forces had struck an Iranian oil tanker off the coast of the strategically important Kharg Island, days after the two sides engaged in the most intense fighting in weeks.

The United States has not confirmed the Iranian reports. A spokesman for the U.S. military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Kharg Island, in the Persian Gulf, is Iran’s primary hub for oil exports, which have been squeezed for weeks by a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian news outlets, including the state broadcaster, said that at least one American missile had hit the tanker, and published images of a ship emitting black plumes of smoke.

Tasnim, a semiofficial news outlet affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, reported that the attack took place on Saturday morning, and that the tanker’s crew had survived and were being evacuated.

The reports come as the fate of the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway on Iran’s southern coast, has become central to the conflict between Iran and the United States. The strait previously served as a major shipping route for oil and other key commodities, but Iran has sought to control it since the country was attacked by the United States and Israel earlier this year.

The U.S. Navy has been helping ships navigate a southern route through the strait, near the coast of Oman, drawing retaliation from Iran. On Monday, two oil tankers were attacked within minutes of each other while trying to pass through.

There had been about a month of relative calm in the conflict between Iran and the United States until late August, when the two sides traded fire. This week, U.S. forces carried out a barrage of strikes in retaliation for Iranian attacks on ships and American forces in the region.

One of the strikes hit a wedding in southern Iran, killing five people and wounding dozens, according to Iranian officials.

President Trump issued a renewed threat to Iran on Friday, saying that the United States may strike Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected Iranian nuclear site, “very soon.”

item.title: U.S. Military Sinks Boats Said to Aid Drug Smuggling Near Ecuador
item.description:
U.S. forces operating near Ecuador on Saturday intercepted and destroyed several commercial vessels believed to be used for refueling boats smuggling drugs to the United States.

It was the fourth interdiction of vessels used as floating refueling platforms in the eastern Pacific, according to a U.S. official, who said no one on either side was hurt or killed.

The mission was carried out as part of U.S. Southern Command’s efforts to hinder narcotics smugglers in the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, a campaign that began just over a year ago.

A video posted to social media by the command, which directs military operations in Central and South America, shows a U.S. military vessel, an 11-meter rigid-hull inflatable boat, approach what appears to be a larger civilian craft with fuel jugs lining a raised open deck. A Marine Corps helicopter hovered off the vessel’s starboard side.

The video shows the inflatable boat moving out of the frame, then shows the larger vessel’s bow erupting in an explosion.

People aboard the refueling vessel were transferred to the custody of Ecuadorean government officials, who were nearby as part of the operation, said the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly about the mission.

The operation was supported by sailors and Marines aboard the amphibious ship U.S.S. San Antonio, which launched helicopters that fired munitions into other accompanying vessels and sank them, the official said.

Southern Command, which is based in South Florida, said the refueling operation was run by Los Choneros, which the State Department designated as a “foreign terrorist organization” just days after the campaign against suspected smuggling vessels began on Sept. 2, 2025.

In that time, the U.S. military has launched 68 attacks on what it said were drug smuggling vessels in the region, killing 227 people, according to a New York Times analysis.

item.title: After Months at War, Brief Solace in a Party Town Far From Home
item.description:
After 286 days at sea, the sailors and Marines of the warship Abraham Lincoln savored the pleasures of Pattaya, Thailand. Their indulgences were not all decadent.

They ate Double Super Cheeseburgers at Burger King. They shopped for LeBron James jerseys at the mall. They sipped from fresh coconuts at the beach, their backs to the water where they had spent the last nine-plus months.

And they danced with scantily clad women at nightclubs, the pounding music seemingly even louder than the aural assault of an aircraft carrier at war.

Pattaya is used to welcoming American servicemen. The beach town grew from an R&R refuge for American military personnel during the Vietnam War. For five days beginning on Wednesday, its pool halls, steakhouses and spas, its go-go bars, burrito shacks and trinket stalls have turned their attention to the 5,000 or so service members from the Lincoln, one of four carriers used in the air campaign against Iran.

After a grueling deployment that fed criticism of the Trump administration’s execution of the war, the service members aboard the Lincoln had been instructed not to speak with members of the news media during their time in Pattaya.

Nevertheless, seven sailors confirmed, on the condition of anonymity, that the carrier’s long months at sea, especially without any of the normal stops at so-called liberty ports, had sapped both supplies and morale. They spoke of clogged toilets and, alarmingly, of multiple suicide attempts. (Navy officials have denied an increase in suicide attempts on the Lincoln.) Amid Iranian missile barrages and drone attacks, the half-day shifts merged into a Sisyphean blur, without the usual relief of care packages from home or treats from the ship store.

Meals were rationed, they said, and offered up a monotony of carbs. What she was really craving, one sailor said, was a salad, something green and fresh. Was there one to be had in Pattaya? There was.

The worst, a sailor from Illinois said, was not knowing how much longer they would be at sea. He stopped counting the days at around 200, despairing that the deployment might never end. Another sailor, a New York native, said that he had gone through a dozen deployments without incident, but this time he had watched junior sailors break, one by one. The price of war, he said, was something he was willing to bear, but not when a logistical crisis, which left the carrier with dwindling supplies, seemed preventable.

Did they, he continued — not defining the “they” — think for a moment about the mental health of those aboard the Lincoln? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said that reports of difficult conditions aboard the Lincoln were “misrepresented.” President Trump opined that the Lincoln’s deployment was “not nearly long enough.”

The residents of Pattaya, at least, appeared to understand the hardship borne by the crew of the Lincoln, which will head next toward its home port, San Diego. Pattaya’s mayor turned up to greet the men and women touching dry land for the first time since November. A gem shop offered discounts to the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps personnel. The Sapphire Club, an adult entertainment venue, dispatched three women in strapless black bodysuits to hold placards offering discounts for those with valid U.S. military ID.

At the Tahitian Queen, which bills itself as the oldest bar in Pattaya, circa 1978, Mickey Foth, one of the owners and an American military veteran and former Pentagon employee, teared up as he considered the sacrifices made by the Lincoln’s personnel.

“It’s not just the physical stress, it’s the emotional toll of such a long deployment,” he said, as a line of women in bikinis, one in an American flag pattern, gyrated onstage. “I want to be here, front and center, to say to these men and women, ‘Thank you for your service.’”

On Thursday night, some of the young sailors blushed amid the sexual maelstrom of Pattaya’s Walking Street, with its touts offering intricate shows involving improbably placed pingpong balls. Others, in the throbbing confines of nightclubs, downed shots and leaned close to female companions. Most of the women were Thai, some were Eastern European and Russian, a few were from neighboring countries like Myanmar and Laos or from as far away as Uganda and Uzbekistan.

Prostitution is illegal in Thailand, but you wouldn’t know it in Pattaya. Ever since American bombing missions took off from a nearby Thai air base during the Vietnam War, the village of Pattaya rapidly expanded its red-light district. Business boomed. With the arrival of the Lincoln, local entrepreneurs talked up the positive effect on Pattaya’s economy.

In earlier decades, some women and girls from Thailand’s poor northeast were sold by their families into sex work in Pattaya. While local aid groups say such human trafficking has waned, the criminalization of prostitution, even as it is openly tolerated, can put prostitutes at the mercy of corrupt forces or periodic crackdowns. In the days leading up to the Lincoln’s docking at a nearby port, the police in Pattaya launched an anti-prostitution raid that, like many before it, seemed to have had little lingering effect, apart from stigmatizing the women.

Today, servicemen are a much smaller demographic in Pattaya, compared to tourists from India, China and the Middle East. Amid the sex shows and vendors selling tubes of personal lubricant, vacationing families toted sleeping children, taking in the scene.

“Pattaya has been able to develop itself as a tourist destination, not only for sex tourism but also for culture, temples, family,” said Chanan Yodhong, a gender and sexual equality activist.

On Thursday night, as some sailors and Marines strolled or sat on the curb reeling from too much to drink, a corps of tourist police stood at attention before scattering into the crowds. There were also volunteer officers, residents who are originally from other parts of Asia, Europe and the Middle East.

Among them was Hooman Peseshk, a native of Iran, who has lived in Pattaya for 10 years. He recognized the irony of his patrolling the streets with a shipful of American sailors returning from the war in Iran. But he loved Pattaya, he said, for its status as a free port, where almost anything goes.

“Nobody wants to fight in a war that was started because of our leaders,” he said. “We are all brothers here in Pattaya.”

Despite the beach town’s reputation, many others from the Lincoln said they had no interest in exploring Play Girlz, KINK or the Harem Ultra go-go club. Instead, they dined poolside at the Hilton. They tried out foot spas where little fish nibbled off calluses. At the Hard Rock Hotel, where the minibar comes stocked with chocolate- and strawberry- flavored condoms, a member of the Lincoln crew said he was planning to spend the night ordering room service for one and watching sports on the big-screen TV.

One sailor said that after so many months aboard the carrier — with its frantic sirens, clattering pipes, screaming jet engines, explosive catapult launches — what he missed most was silence. Pattaya is many things, but it is not quiet. For that the sailor would have to wait.

John Ismay contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Chinese Worker Rescued From Tunnel in Nepal 10 Days After Floods
item.description:
A Chinese worker was rescued on Saturday from a tunnel in Nepal, the Nepali Army said, 10 days after its entrance was buried in the catastrophic floods that tore through one of the country’s northern river systems.

The army said that a joint rescue team, including foreign personnel, had pulled the man from inside a 740-foot tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project. “His health is currently being assessed, and further search and rescue operations are continuing,” the army said in a statement. It did not immediately confirm the man’s name.

At least 1,200 people were killed in the disaster last week, when a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent tsunami-like waves through valleys along the border of Nepal and the Tibet region of China. Another 5,000 people are missing.

Rescue efforts in recent days have become focused on the hundreds of men who were working underground at the time of the disaster, building the power stations that form the basis of Nepal’s budding hydropower industry.

Unlike the thousands of people who were living alongside the rivers, the workers trapped underground, it was hoped, might have been able to shelter from the force of the flood and find enough air and fresh water to survive beyond the 72-hour window after which rescuers estimate that the chances of survival usually drop off.

On Friday, that hope was at least partially vindicated when two Nepali workers were found alive in a tunnel below the Upper Trishuli 3A project, downriver from the site of Saturday’s rescue. One of the men, Sanjay Sah, estimated that there had been 40 or 50 others at his work site when the disaster struck. He knew of no others who might still be living, he said.

In February, the deputy director of the labor ministry in Nepal told local media outlets that about 1,600 Chinese citizens were living in Nepal on work permits. That made China the biggest source of foreign workers in Nepal — not counting India, which sends its citizens back and forth across the Nepali border freely.

Chinese engineers are especially visible at Nepal’s hydropower and other infrastructure projects.

South Korea has an especially large investment in the Upper Trishuli-1 project, one of the most productive hydropower plants in the area. A 44-member Korea Disaster Relief Team has been working in the afflicted districts of Nepal since Tuesday.

item.title: Trump Envoys Arrive in Moscow for Talks on Ukraine War
item.description:
President Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday, Russian state news agencies reported, ahead of a planned trip to Kyiv, Ukraine, as they hope to reignite diplomatic efforts to end the war there.

Mr. Witkoff, the president’s special envoy, and Mr. Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, are making their first trip to Russia since January. A month after that visit, U.S.-backed peace negotiations went into a deep freeze when the United States and Israel attacked Iran.

Since Mr. Trump took office in January 2025, Mr. Witkoff has met regularly with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. At the end of that year, Mr. Kushner began joining Mr. Witkoff for meetings with the Russian leader.

But the planned trip to Kyiv would be the first by either American envoy.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said on Friday that Ukrainian forces would not conduct airstrikes on Russia while the envoys were there, and he called on Mr. Putin to reciprocate by temporarily halting strikes on Ukraine.

The U.S. envoys’ visit to the Russian capital is taking place days after the C.I.A. director, John Ratcliffe, traveled there. Mr. Ratcliffe delivered a bleak assessment of Moscow’s prospects in the war and urged Russian officials to end it.

The talks follow a shift in the war’s dynamics. Since April, Ukraine has launched a campaign targeting Russian fuel and logistics infrastructure, bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians.

Russia, for its part, has taken advantage of Ukraine’s depleted arsenal of air defense interceptors, allowing it to strike more targets across the country and making daily life in Kyiv increasingly dangerous. On Friday, a drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s domestic intelligence service in the heart of the Ukrainian capital.

Russia and Ukraine also face mounting financial strain to support a war that is growing costlier, as both sides struggle to keep pace with advanced technologies, like jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles.

But the war appears far away from any resolution.

Speaking on Friday, Dmitri S. Peskov, Mr. Putin’s spokesman, praised “the good will of the Americans” who, he said, “are ready to continue their mediation efforts.” But Mr. Peskov said Russia would continue to insist that Ukraine withdraw its troops from the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, in the country’s east, before any cease-fire could occur — a demand that Ukraine has rejected.

Mr. Peskov’s comments followed statements on Thursday by Mr. Putin, who said that regardless of American mediation efforts, “Russia and Ukraine must first reach an agreement between themselves.”

item.title: Here Is Where Ukraine Peace Talks Stand, as a New Round Approaches
item.description:
Trump administration envoys arrived on Saturday in Moscow in an effort to restart talks to end the war between Russia and Ukraine, over six months after a previous round of discussions fizzled out.

The trip by Steve Witkoff, the administration’s peace envoy, and Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, came even as Russian and Ukrainian forces are locked in an escalating spiral of airstrikes.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said on Thursday that U.S. envoys would “have a meeting in Moscow and another one in Kyiv,” Ukraine’s capital. He added: “It is important that America remain actively engaged. We are ready to meet with them in Ukraine — properly and substantively.”

Kyrylo Budanov, the Ukrainian delegation’s leader at the previous talks, told The New York Times in a recent interview that negotiations mediated by the Trump administration were expected to begin by late September, days after Russia’s parliamentary election and weeks before U.S. midterm elections.

It is not clear whether a new round of talks will yield more progress than previous ones. But “negotiations will sooner or later come to something,” Mr. Budanov told The Times. “You cannot fight your whole life.”

Here is what to know about peace talks and where they stand.

Russia and Ukraine have been talking at various levels since February 2022, when Russian forces mounted a full-scale invasion of Ukrainian territory. Despite brief cease-fires and occasional prisoner swaps, the two sides have made little headway toward ending the war.

A new flurry of high-level, U.S.-brokered negotiations began shortly after Mr. Trump — who claimed he could end the war in a day — took office in January 2025.

The last round of face-to-face talks was held in February, when Ukrainian and Russian negotiators met in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, and then later in Geneva. But there was no breakthrough in those discussions, and they ground to a halt after the United States and Israel went to war against Iran, a conflict that has consumed the Trump administration’s attention.

Since then, there have been limited contacts between Moscow and Kyiv, but the major issues have remained on hold.

In June, Mr. Zelensky published an open letter to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia that offered to resume peace talks, but that also taunted the Russian leader. Mr. Putin, who has shown little serious interest in peace negotiations, recently pledged to pursue the war.

The last round of negotiations focused a 20-point peace plan that covered a broad range of issues, including security guarantees that Ukraine seeks to prevent future Russian aggression, and commitments to rebuild the war-ravaged nation.

But the two sides have struggled to reach common ground on several crucial points, including the possible deployment of Western forces in Ukraine, control of territory in the country’s east, and management of a Russian-occupied nuclear power plant.

Russia has demanded that Ukraine hand over the land it controls in the eastern Donetsk region as a condition for ending the war, a strip of territory about 50 miles long and 40 miles wide that includes dozens of towns and villages. Ukraine has refused to withdraw unilaterally, arguing that ceding land would embolden Russia to attack again, and it has asked for guarantees that would deter Moscow from violating any cease-fire.

The United States has been the main mediator in talks between Russia and Ukraine.

But European leaders — nervous that Mr. Trump will cut them out of any settlement — are trying to take a more active role in ending the war, whose outcome could shape the continent’s security for decades to come. Mr. Trump has also made it clear that he sees Ukraine as a European responsibility.

European diplomats are working on a format for future negotiations to protect European interests that would be led by France, Germany and Britain, European officials said last month.

The front, stretching hundreds of miles through eastern Ukraine, has largely been frozen. The terrain has been devastated, a killing field dominated by drones, making troop movement a lethal risk.

As a result, Russia and Ukraine have instead intensified a campaign of airstrikes that have caused death and destruction in cities far from the battlefield. Over the summer, the two sides have launched drones and missiles at energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and ports that are crucial to grain exports.

Note: As of Aug. 3. Includes Ukrainian drone and missile attacks inside Russia. Strikes within 60 miles of the border are not shown. Source: Armed Conflict Location & Event Data. The New York Times

Russia has pummeled Kyiv with unrelenting daytime attacks of new jet-powered drones, taking advantage of a Ukrainian shortage of air defenses. Ukraine has launched attacks increasingly deep into Russia’s territory, disrupting its economy and isolating Crimea.

Even if negotiations resume this month, conditions for a cease-fire are unlikely to come until spring, Mr. Budanov told The Times. Russia is expected to attempt to break Ukraine in another strategic winter bombing campaign, the fourth of the war.

More than two million Russian and Ukrainian troops have been killed or wounded in the four years that Russia has been waging war against its neighbor, according to one study.
